# ernd: the credit card for the AI stack

Get faster inference, better access to GPUs, and 4% back on AI

Connor Dawson

ernd

#ai#fintech

ernd is the credit card for companies that pay for AI. Cardholders earn 4% back on AI spend, and benefit from partnerships for better pricing and capacity, like faster inference or dedicated GPUs.

The problem  
 When we tried to get GPUs earlier in the batch, we were met with terrible deals or no capacity because we didn’t have enough size. Providers save their best pricing, limits and capacity for their biggest customers.

The solution

We go to providers on behalf of everyone on the card. By paying with ernd, you get access to better rates and top-tier perks. Priority GPUs and inference are coming soon. [...] Who we are  
 Connor built an AI forecasting system at Bridgewater’s AIA Labs. Nikhil worked on data infrastructure at IMC Trading and payments at Ripple. Malcolm founded an investment fund and built AI agents for finance at a Series A startup. We’re also credit card nerds, each having 5 cards we rotate to maximize points!

The ask  
 If your company pays for AI, request a card at ernd.io. There’s no annual fee and we’ll get you the deals you deserve. If you’d like to partner with us, reach out at ernd.io/partners :)

results.title: AI Agents Got Credit Cards. Nobody Built the Fraud Stack.
results.content:

Alexandra Dawood, MBA, graphic

Alexandra Dawood, MBA   7mo 

 Report this comment

Great read! The AI agents using credit cards scenario is a clear case of technical debt because companies and teams have prioritized short‑term delivery over maintainable design, which is now driving higher change costs, slower releases, and increased risk to data quality and system reliability. As product and data stakeholders, we need to consciously allocate capacity for refactoring, test automation, and platform improvements to reduce this technical debt and regain predictable delivery.

Like Reply  1 Reaction   2 Reactions

PromptBridge, graphic

PromptBridge   7mo 

 Report this comment [...] There is also the authorization scope problem. When a person uses a card, the authorization is implicit: I am the cardholder, I am present, I am approving this transaction. When an agent uses a card, the authorization is delegated: someone told the agent it could spend money, but the exact scope of that delegation is stored in a system the card network has no access to. A transaction that exceeds the intended authorization scope may still pass every fraud check, because the fraud system has no way to query the delegation record. [...] AI agents can now hold payment credentials. They can initiate transactions. They can buy software licenses, book travel, pay invoices, and renew subscriptions without a human in the loop. Stripe and Tempo's Machine Payments Protocol, launched March 18, created a native API for exactly this. Visa shipped a command-line tool that lets agents trigger card payments programmatically. Mastercard acquired BVNK for $1.8 billion to own the stablecoin bridge underneath the whole stack.

The rails exist. The credentials exist. The authorization mechanism exists.

What doesn't exist is a fraud and trust framework built for non-human buyers.

results.title: Opinion: AI Is Making Credit Card Fraud More Difficult to Detect and Stop
results.content:
The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center received 22,364 internet crime complaints that contained references to AI in 2025. And AI-related losses have reached a staggering $893 million and aren’t slowing down.

Consumers face a growing number of phishing scams, fake customer service calls, and deepfake videos that look and sound frighteningly like the real thing.

The difference is that scams today look so real, they can get consumers to authorize transactions or submit payments they did not intend. To safeguard security, financial institutions add more protections, which make legitimate transactions more complex.

022,364  AI crime complaints in 2025, per the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center [...] Follow Us: 287 1,236

Artificial intelligence has moved out of the pilot phase in the finance space and is now deep into application. Among its many functions, it’s used to approve loan and credit card applications, detect fraud, provide customer service, and monitor spending patterns.

On the surface, the benefits seem to go on and on. But the deeper AI moves into the financial system, the more consumers realize that convenience comes with new risks, fewer human interactions, and a sense of losing control.

The general consensus is that AI has improved efficiency and productivity. Transactions happen quicker, decisions on credit cards are faster, and security alerts are instantaneous. At the same time, this technology has also ushered in some new problems. [...] Remote transactions expose you to AI-generated synthetic identities such as false profiles stolen from invented data; deepfake verification artifacts like simulated videos and voices; and personalized phishing that can be almost undetectable from the real thing.

Avoiding AI scams is everyone’s business, and while expensive to deploy, building defensive measures is an investment in sound business practice.

Personal and institutional losses due to fraud cost more. Consumers aren’t the only party that needs to pay attention to expenses.
